evidence.quote: below 715 °C, heating rate of 100°C/min, pressure of 5 MPa; then, within 1 min, temperature is increased from 715 to 750 °C and pressure is increased from 5 to 50 MPa, followed by heating at a rate of 50°C/min to 800°C, 900°C, 1000°C, and 1100°C, respectively (four sets of samples are named G800, G900, G1000, and G1100); the dwell time is 10 min, quenching upon sintering completion, and the entire sintering process is carried out under vacuum (less than 10 Pa).

The HRTEM and SAED confirm that the matrix phase is an FCC phase in the (Ref 0-11) direction and the twins are in the (Ref 110) direction of the matrix phase.

The oxide observed in Fig. 5b is mainly enriched in Cr and Mn. Due to the large difference in electronegativity between Cr, Mn, and O, they readily form a stable intermediate phase CrMn1.5O4 (Ref 40).

When sintered at 800 °C and 900 °C, the presence of micropores is observed, as depicted in Figure 3b. The formation of these micropores is primarily attributed to insufficient sintering due to the low sintering temperature, leading to compromised mechanical properties and density of the bulk alloy (Ref 36).
It can also be observed that plate-like annealing twins are formed in different CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples (at the point indicated by the black arrow in IPF maps).
Fig 5a and b show the main microstructures including the FCC matrix phase, oxide precipitates, pronounced twins, and dislocations (yellow markings in Fig 5a and b.

The accumulation of dislocations leads to an increase in local stress and promotes the formation of deformation twins, which contribute to the alloy’s enhanced mechanical properties in terms of deformation capacity and work-hardening ability (Ref 39). Deformation twins are a crucial mechanism for enhancing the alloy’s strength and ductility by accommodating the stress and strain that result from external forces.
